tweets: One teacher's grudge against a king rewrote the map of India — and gave it its first great empire.

Chanakya, a scholar humiliated by the Nanda king of Magadha, vowed revenge. He found his instrument in a young man named Chandragupta and trained him in statecraft — strategy later distilled into the treatise Arthashastra.

Around 321 BCE, Chandragupta's forces toppled the mighty Nanda dynasty and seized Pataliputra. Crowned ruler of the Maurya Empire, he built India's first pan-Indian state, soon stretching from Bengal to Afghanistan.

In 305 BCE he even stood up to Alexander's heir. Chandragupta fought Seleucus I Nicator to a standstill — the peace treaty won him vast northwestern territory, in exchange for 500 war elephants and a marriage alliance.

Late in life he gave up the throne, embraced Jain monkhood, and walked to Shravanabelagola, where tradition holds he ended his days in fasting meditation. An empire won by ambition, surrendered in peace. Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history. 🏛️
